damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 21 (Shell Cottage cliff) — Harry explains the mirror shard to Ron
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book (DH ch.7/10), the mirror shard is a fragment of the two-way mirror Sirius gave Harry in OotP. Harry keeps it because it is one of the few remaining physical traces of Sirius; it is an object of grief and longing. He carries it in the mokeskin purse alongside the Marauder's Map and the fake locket — items he prizes. The shard later connects to Aberforth, but Harry never knows this during the horcrux hunt; he simply sees what he believes is Dumbledore's eye and is comforted/confused by it.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 21 has Harry explicitly explain the mirror to Ron: 'Sirius gave it to me. He had a matching piece. He said if I ever needed him, all I had to do was look into it.' Harry then says he thinks he has seen Dumbledore in it. This compresses and distorts the emotional history of the object: in the books Harry never successfully used it while Sirius was alive and is haunted by that failure (Sirius died partly because Harry did not use the mirror instead of flying to the DoM). The film strips the guilt dimension entirely, recasting the shard as a straightforwardly useful communication tool Harry simply forgot to use, rather than a symbol of his failure and grief.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Sirius's gift of the mirror and Harry's failure to use it is a key node of Harry's guilt over Sirius's death. By presenting the mirror as something Harry just 'never got to use' without any guilt framing, the film loses the emotional weight Sirius's death carries into Deathly Hallows and weakens the ongoing cost of that loss.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 (Sirius's room, Grimmauld Place) — Harry in the room
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book DH ch.10 describes Sirius's room in rich detail: Gryffindor banners deliberately provocative toward his Slytherin family, Muggle motorcycle posters, posters of bikini-clad Muggle girls (stationary, proving they are Muggle), and crucially a photograph of the four Marauders — young, happy, 'carelessly handsome' Sirius with 'slightly arrogant face so much younger and happier than Harry had ever seen it alive.' Harry also finds Lily's letter to Sirius, searches desperately for the rest, and finds the torn photograph of baby Harry on a broomstick. The room establishes Sirius's personality, his rebelliousness, his deep friendship with James, and his bond with the Potters.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 3 reduces the room visit to Harry briefly pausing at a photograph of the four Marauders at the Whomping Willow and finding Lily's letter on the floor. The Gryffindor banners, the Muggle girl posters (which signal Sirius's personality and his rebellion), the motorcycle posters, and the frantic search for the rest of the letter and the torn baby-Harry photograph are all absent. The room is just 'ransacked' with books scattered.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The bedroom is the primary corpus evidence for Sirius's youthful personality in DH — his wit, nerve, rebelliousness, love of Muggles, and defiant affection for James. Stripping it to a bare ransacked space removes almost all of this characterisation. The book's Sirius is vividly present in his room even in death; the film's version makes the room functionally inert.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 6 (Kitchen, Grimmauld Place) — Kreacher interrogation about the locket
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book DH ch.10: Harry questions Kreacher at length. Kreacher tells the full story of being taken to the cave by Voldemort, drinking the potion, the Inferi, escaping via house-elf magic, and Regulus's subsequent heroic self-sacrifice. Harry watches Kreacher weep and is moved. Hermione explains that Sirius was 'horrible to Kreacher' and that Kreacher betrayed Sirius because Sirius never treated him as a being with feelings — a direct moral indictment of Sirius. Harry has 'no retort' and remembers Dumbledore's words: 'I do not think Sirius ever saw Kreacher as a being with feelings as acute as a human's.' Harry then shows Kreacher the fake locket as a gift, which transforms Kreacher's loyalty. The whole scene is a moral reckoning about how Sirius's cruelty contributed to his own death.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 6 has Kreacher give only a brief, functional account: Regulus ordered him to destroy the locket, he could not, Mundungus took it. There is no account of the cave, no weeping, no Hermione speech about Sirius's cruelty, no moral reckoning. Harry simply orders Kreacher to find Mundungus and Kreacher vanishes. Ron grabs Kreacher by the neck and shakes him — the opposite of the book's moment of empathy.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This scene is the primary moment in DH where Sirius's moral failure is explicitly examined by other characters and by Harry himself. Its omission removes the only substantive critical perspective on Sirius in the book corpus, erases the causal link between Sirius's treatment of Kreacher and his death, and eliminates the thematic argument about how wizards' treatment of house-elves has consequences. Sirius's agency in his own death (via his cruelty) is completely lost, which distorts audience understanding of his character's flaws.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 23 (Hogsmeade/Aberforth's pub) — explanation of the mirror shard provenance
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book DH: Aberforth has the twin mirror because Mundungus stole it from Grimmauld Place after Sirius's death. Harry is angry that Dung sold it — 'It belonged to Sirius.' This beat reaffirms the emotional significance of the mirror as Sirius's possession and Harry's continuing possessiveness of anything connected to his godfather.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 23 includes Aberforth saying 'Sirius. Albus told me.' and Harry saying 'Dung had no right selling you that. It belonged to —' which is faithful to that beat. However, the scene is brief and Harry's anger is quickly redirected. This scene is largely faithful and causes minimal damage.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The line is present and broadly faithful. Damage is minimal — Harry's emotional connection to Sirius's possessions is at least partially conveyed, though the depth of grief is not elaborated.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 29 (Snape's memories — Great Hall sorting) — Sirius and James at Gryffindor table
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book DH ch.33 ('The Prince's Tale'): At the sorting, Sirius nudges along the bench to make room for Lily when she is sorted into Gryffindor. Lily takes one look at him, 'seemed to recognise him from the train, folded her arms, and firmly turned her back on him.' This establishes that even as an eleven-year-old Sirius had already made a bad impression on Lily, consistent with his arrogance on the train. It also shows James's immediate attraction to Lily and Sirius's easy social dominance.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 29 shows Sirius and James at the Gryffindor table watching the sorting. James nudges Sirius to move over and make space for Lily. Lily sits down and glances across at Snape. The beat of Lily recognising Sirius from the train and turning her back on him is absent. Sirius is a mostly silent background figure.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book beat is small but establishes that Sirius's arrogance was apparent even to Lily from the very first moment at Hogwarts. Its absence is a minor omission but consistent with the film's overall pattern of smoothing Sirius's rougher edges.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 32 (Forbidden Forest) — Sirius with the Resurrection Stone
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book DH ch.34: Sirius appears via the Resurrection Stone. He is described as 'tall and handsome, and younger by far than Harry had ever seen him in life. He loped with an easy grace, his hands in his pockets and a grin on his face.' He tells Harry dying is 'Quicker and easier than falling asleep.' He says 'We are part of you. Invisible to anyone else.' His characterisation here is confident, warm, and physically graceful — his youth and ease restored. He is also specifically Sirius, with his own voice and bearing distinct from James or Lupin.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 32 shows Sirius (as Sirius Black) appearing with James, Lupin, and Lily. He delivers the line 'Quicker than falling asleep' (faithful). He shakes his head when Harry asks if Voldemort will see them, gestures to Harry's heart, says 'No. We're here, you see.' His characterisation is broadly faithful in this brief appearance. The 'grin,' the 'loping easy grace,' the 'hands in his pockets' physical detail is not filmically elaborable in the same way but the spirit is present. This scene is largely faithful.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Forest scene is one of the most faithful Sirius moments in the film corpus. Some of the physical characterisation detail from the book is necessarily lost in translation to film, but the emotional content and Sirius's lines are preserved. Damage is minimal.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 15 (Lovegood house) — Harry names Sirius when choosing the Resurrection Stone
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book DH ch.21: Harry says he would choose the Stone because 'we could have Sirius...Mad-Eye...Dumbledore...my parents.' Sirius is named first, reflecting his primacy among Harry's lost loved ones. The context also includes Hermione's warning that according to the tale the dead would not want to come back — which connects to the later Forest scene.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 15: Harry says 'Well, you could bring people back, couldn't you? Mad-Eye. Dumbledore. Sirius. Anybody.' Sirius is named third rather than first, and the order 'Mad-Eye. Dumbledore. Sirius.' subtly repositions Sirius as less primary among Harry's dead. This is a very minor ordering change.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Extremely minor. The book names Sirius first, emphasising his special place among Harry's losses; the film lists him third. The difference is marginal and does not substantially alter the scene's meaning. Included for completeness but damage is negligible.

main_damage_causes: Omission of the Kreacher confrontation scene's moral reckoning removes the only explicit critique of Sirius's cruelty in the DH narrative, erasing the causal link between his treatment of Kreacher and his death and eliminating his most significant character flaw as examined posthumously

Reduction of Sirius's bedroom from a richly characterised space (Gryffindor banners, Muggle posters, evidence of rebellious personality) to a generic ransacked room strips the primary posthumous characterisation of young Sirius available in this portion of the story

The mirror shard's emotional weight — specifically Harry's guilt at never having used it while Sirius was alive — is absent from the film, recasting the object as a neutral tool rather than a symbol of Harry's failure and ongoing grief
